title: Given an n×n adjacency matrix where isConnected[i][j] = 1 means city i and city j are directly connected, return the number of provinces (connected groups of cities).
shortTitle: Number of Provinces — count friend circles via Union-Find

s1_definition.profdef: Treat the symmetric adjacency matrix as an undirected graph over n cities. Start the province count at n and union every pair (i, j) where isConnected[i][j] equals one; each successful union decrements the count. The remaining count is the number of connected components, i.e., provinces.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India groups its regional hubs into provinces based on who shares a direct data line. If hub i and hub j share a line they are in the same province, and provinces grow transitively. Count the hubs, merge every directly connected pair, and whatever separate groups remain are the provinces.
s1_definition.oneliner: Start at n, union every connected pair in the matrix, and the leftover count is the number of provinces.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Treat the symmetric adjacency matrix as an undirected graph over n cities. Start the province count at n and union every pair (i, j) where isConnected[i][j] equals one; each successful union decrements the count. The remaining count is the number of connected components, i.e., provinces.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India groups its regional hubs into provinces based on who shares a direct data line. If hub i and hub j share a line they are in the same province, and provinces grow transitively. Count the hubs, merge every directly connected pair, and whatever separate groups remain are the provinces.

**One line to remember:** Start at n, union every connected pair in the matrix, and the leftover count is the number of provinces.

sections.s2_technical:
Initialize Union-Find over n cities with the count set to n. Scan the upper triangle of the matrix to avoid redundant work, since it is symmetric. For example: `for (int i=0;i<n;i++) for (int j=i+1;j<n;j++) if (m[i][j]==1 && union(i,j)) count--;`.

Each one in the matrix that links two cities in different sets reduces the count; a one between already-connected cities changes nothing. The diagonal is always one (a city is connected to itself) and is simply skipped by starting j at i+1.

The time is n squared because the whole matrix is scanned, with near-constant union cost per edge, and the space is the parent and rank arrays. A senior nuance is that if the input were an edge list rather than a dense matrix, the time would drop to the number of edges, so the n-squared cost here is a property of the dense input representation, not of Union-Find.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, regional data hubs are connected by direct lines described in a connectivity matrix, and the network team needs to know how many independent provinces exist so each province gets one failover plan. This is exactly how counting provinces works.

Problem 2 — A direct line between two hubs already in the same province does not create a new province. This is exactly why a union only decrements the count on a real merge.

The mini-project builds a `ProvinceCounter`, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is a three-by-three connectivity matrix for three hubs.

Step 1: The count starts at three, one per hub.

Step 2: The scan finds isConnected[0][1] equals one, so hubs zero and one union and the count drops to two.

Step 3: No connection links hub two to the others, so it stays its own province.

Step 4: The final count is two provinces: the group of hubs zero and one, and hub two alone.

```text
2026-10-26T23:40:00Z [INFO] National Bank of India — Hub Province Counter
2026-10-26T23:40:00Z [INFO] Hub 0 joined hub 1; provinces=2
2026-10-26T23:40:00Z [INFO] Total provinces: 2
2026-10-26T23:40:00Z [INFO] Provinces = 2
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  cities {0}{1}{2}  count=3
    scan upper triangle:
      m[0][1]=1 → union(0,1) → count=2
      m[0][2]=0, m[1][2]=0 → no change
  provinces = 2  → {0,1} , {2}
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Number of Provinces is Union-Find applied to a symmetric adjacency matrix. I start a province counter at n, because each of the n cities begins in its own group, and then I scan the matrix unioning every pair of cities marked as directly connected. I scan only the upper triangle since the matrix is symmetric, and I skip the diagonal because a city is trivially connected to itself. Every union that merges two previously separate groups decrements the counter by one.

When the scan completes, the counter holds the number of connected components, which is the number of provinces. The cost is n squared because the dense matrix must be fully scanned, with each edge costing only the near-constant Union-Find operation; if the input were an edge list instead, it would drop to the number of edges.

In my project at National Bank of India, regional data hubs were described by a connectivity matrix and the network team needed the number of independent provinces so each province could get its own failover plan. Union-Find gave a clean count, and because a direct line between two hubs already in the same province never created a spurious new group, the number of failover plans we provisioned stayed exactly right.
